query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Nitrogen doping of a near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy automotive catalyst will create a Pt‐rich surface with multiple metal–nitrogen bonds that improve low‐temperature oxidation activity, enhance resistance against poisoning (e.g., by H2O and NO), and extend long-term durability without increasing platinum-group-metal loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst (e.g., a PtCoFeNiCu system) with low platinum-group-metal use and a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled nitrogen doping via a thermal annealing process followed by acid-etching dealloying to induce the formation of a Pt-rich shell and multiple metal–nitrogen bonds within the HEA lattice.
generation.conditions: Catalytic oxidation tests under automotive exhaust conditions at low to moderate temperatures (below 150 °C), with transient exposure to poisons such as H2O and NO, combined with accelerated aging protocols that mimic vehicle lifetime mileage.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a Pt-rich surface layer reinforced by in situ generated metal–nitrogen bonds in the alloy core.
generation.mechanism: Nitrogen incorporation promotes the formation of stable M–N bonds that modify the electronic structure and lattice strain, thereby stabilizing the catalyst against sintering and deactivation, tuning the adsorption energies of reactants/intermediates, and mitigating CO and other poisoning species from binding too strongly.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, the N-doped HEA is expected to show enhanced low-temperature oxidation activity, improved poisoning resistance, and superior long-term durability while maintaining low platinum usage.
generation.baseline: The original near-equiatomic automotive HEA catalyst without nitrogen doping, which suffers from degradation (sintering, poisoning) during transient low-temperature operation and extended exposure to exhaust conditions.
generation.boundary: This improvement is predicted to hold under conditions similar to standard automotive exhaust environments; however, excessive nitrogen levels or improper processing may lead to detrimental effects, and the magnitude of enhancement may vary with the exact HEA composition and processing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in activity and lifetime durability under real-world conditions is uncertain and requires experimental validation. The optimal nitrogen content and processing conditions must be fine-tuned to avoid potential over-doping effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of near-equiatomic automotive HEA catalysts: one set undergoes the proposed nitrogen doping (thermal annealing plus acid-etching) and the other remains undoped. Subject both sets to catalytic oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons under simulated automotive exhaust conditions (temperature range 100–150 °C, with controlled H2O and NO concentrations) and accelerated aging tests (continuous operation over extended time to mimic vehicle lifetime). Structural characterization (XRD, HAADF-STEM/EDS, XPS) should be performed pre- and post-testing to evaluate Pt surface enrichment and the formation of M–N bonds.
measurements: Light-off temperature (T50, T10) for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation
CO and NO tolerance (activity retention in the presence of these species)
Long-term durability (activity retention over time under accelerated aging conditions)
Structural stability via XRD and STEM imaging to assess sintering and phase changes
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrogen-doped HEA catalyst does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 10% reduction in light-off temperature and higher activity retention after aging) compared to the undoped catalyst, or shows evidence of accelerated sintering/degradation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

We successfully synthesized the N–Pt/HEA catalyst with a Pt-rich shell and a high entropy alloy PtCoFeNiCu core with multiple M–N bonds via a facile thermal annealing process and an acid-etching de-alloying strategy. The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst possesses a unique structure and electrochemical stability, resulting in excellent long-term durability under HDV conditions. Detailed studies on atomic structure utilizing in situ synchrotron XRD and XAS, coupled with HAADF-STEM/EDS and DFT calculations, allowed the elucidation of influencing factors on the catalytic properties and performance of the novel catalyst. The high performance of N–Pt/HEA/C originates from the combined effect of high entropy, multiple M-N bonds, and a Pt-rich shell. In addition to the enhancement of corrosion resistance, the M–N bonds through N-doping can boost the activity and durability of the electrocatalyst by the distortion effect in the core structure. The synergy between the three factors further endows the N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst to outperform the state-of-the-art Pt/C electrocatalysts and most binary/ternary Pt-based catalysts for the ORR.
